chapters.title: I Am of Paul
chapters.teaser: Paul opens by naming the exact factions splitting the Corinthian church into rival camps.
body: "Every one of you saith, I am of Paul; and I of Apollos; and I of Cephas; and I of Christ" (v.12). This isn't abstract theology — it's Paul quoting the actual slogans dividing a congregation that had turned its leaders into brand loyalties.

"Is Christ divided? was Paul crucified for you?" (v.13) exposes the absurdity with two sharp questions. The chapter's entire argument — about wisdom, the cross, and God's choice of the lowly — is Paul's attempt to knock out the foundation underneath status-seeking factionalism before it can do more damage.

chapters.title: Foolishness That Saves
chapters.teaser: Paul calls the cross foolish on purpose, before explaining why that foolishness is actually power.
body: "The preaching of the cross is to them that perish foolishness; but unto us which are saved it is the power of God" (v.18). A crucified savior was a scandal in the ancient world — crucifixion was a criminal's death, not a hero's. Paul doesn't dodge that; he leans into it.

"I will destroy the wisdom of the wise" (v.19), quoting Isaiah, sets up the chapter's real target: not intellect itself, but intellect used as a status marker. The cross doesn't compete with worldly wisdom on its own terms — it bypasses the whole system of impressiveness the Corinthians were ranking their teachers by.

chapters.title: Signs and Wisdom
chapters.teaser: Paul says Christ crucified fails to satisfy either of the two things his audience was actually looking for.
body: "The Jews require a sign, and the Greeks seek after wisdom: but we preach Christ crucified, unto the Jews a stumblingblock, and unto the Greeks foolishness" (v.22–23). Neither audience got what it wanted — no display of power, no polished philosophy.

"Unto them which are called...Christ the power of God, and the wisdom of God" (v.24) is the twist: the very thing that disappoints both expectations turns out to fulfill them both, just not in the form anyone was watching for. The mismatch between expectation and fulfillment is the chapter's real subject.

chapters.title: Not Many Wise, Not Many Noble
chapters.teaser: Paul points at the Corinthian church itself as evidence for how God tends to choose people.
body: "Ye see your calling, brethren, how that not many wise men after the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble, are called" (v.26). This wasn't abstract theory for the Corinthians — Paul is describing the actual sociology of the room reading this letter.

"God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise...that no flesh should glory in his presence" (v.27, 29). The pattern isn't incidental; it's designed to prevent exactly the kind of status competition — I'm with the more impressive teacher — that opened the chapter.

chapters.title: Glory in the Lord
chapters.teaser: The chapter closes by relocating the church's boasting from leaders to Christ alone.
body: "Of him are ye in Christ Jesus, who of God is made unto us wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption" (v.30). Everything the Corinthians were chasing through rival teachers — wisdom, standing, moral cleanliness — Paul says is already theirs in Christ.

"He that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord" (v.31), quoting Jeremiah, gives the whole chapter its final instruction. It doesn't erase Paul, Apollos, or Cephas as legitimate teachers — it just removes them as objects of the boasting that started the fight in verse 12.

chapters.title: Nothing but Christ Crucified
chapters.teaser: Paul says he deliberately stripped his message down to its barest, least impressive form.
body: "I determined not to know any thing among you, save Jesus Christ, and him crucified" (v.2). Given that chapter 1 just diagnosed a taste for polished rhetoric, this is a pointed choice — Paul refusing to compete on Corinth's preferred terms.

"I came not with excellency of speech or of wisdom" (v.1) reinforces the same restraint. It's not that Paul lacked eloquence — later evidence suggests otherwise — but that he judged eloquence a liability here, something that could let people believe in his skill rather than in the message itself.

chapters.title: Weakness as Credential
chapters.teaser: Paul offers his own fear and trembling as proof that the message's power wasn't his doing.
body: "I was with you in weakness, and in fear, and in much trembling. And my speech and my preaching was not with enticing words of man's wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power" (v.3–4).

"That your faith should not stand in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God" (v.5) explains the strategy: if Paul had persuaded through charisma, the Corinthians' faith would rest on him. By minimizing his own polish, he tries to make sure what convinces them can't be credited to the messenger.

chapters.title: What Eye Has Not Seen
chapters.teaser: Paul says the deepest truths of the gospel were never available through ordinary observation.
body: "Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither have entered into the heart of man, the things which God hath prepared for them that love him. But God hath revealed them unto us by his Spirit" (v.9–10). Human perception, however sharp, simply isn't the right tool for this kind of knowledge.

This directly undercuts the Corinthian obsession with impressive wisdom — if the content in question was never accessible to unaided human insight in the first place, then rhetorical brilliance was never going to be the way to reach it. Only revelation gets there.

chapters.title: The Spirit Searches Everything
chapters.teaser: Paul compares the Spirit's knowledge of God to a person's private knowledge of their own mind.
body: "What man knoweth the things of a man, save the spirit of man which is in him? even so the things of God knoweth no man, but the Spirit of God" (v.11). The analogy is intimate — the only reliable access to someone's inner thoughts is their own spirit; the same logic applies, on a far larger scale, to knowing God.

"We have received, not the spirit of the world, but the spirit which is of God; that we might know the things that are freely given to us of God" (v.12). The passage builds toward a claim of genuine access — not secondhand guesswork about God, but insight made possible by the Spirit's own searching.

chapters.title: The Mind of Christ
chapters.teaser: Paul ends the chapter with an audacious claim about what believers actually possess.
body: "Who hath known the mind of the Lord, that he may instruct him? But we have the mind of Christ" (v.16), quoting Isaiah's rhetorical question and then answering it with something that sounds almost too bold to say plainly.

It's a fitting close to a chapter built entirely around inversion: the foolish message turns out wise, the weak preacher turns out powerful, and ordinary believers — not the polished philosophers Corinth admired — turn out to possess a mind no merely human wisdom could have supplied on its own.

chapters.title: Milk, Not Meat
chapters.teaser: Paul diagnoses the Corinthians' quarreling as proof they're still spiritual infants.
body: "I have fed you with milk, and not with meat: for hitherto ye were not able to bear it" (v.2). The measure of spiritual maturity here isn't knowledge level — it's whether "envying, and strife, and divisions" (v.3) still run the room.

"Are ye not carnal, and walk as men?" (v.3) is a pointed jab: people who claim spiritual sophistication while behaving exactly like anyone else, ruled by rivalry, haven't actually grown as much as they think. The factionalism from chapter 1 gets its diagnosis here — not lack of information, but lack of maturity.

chapters.title: Planting and Watering
chapters.teaser: Paul demotes himself and Apollos from rival leaders to mere farmhands under God's actual work.
body: "I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase. So then neither is he that planteth any thing, neither he that watereth; but God that giveth the increase" (v.6–7). The agricultural image deliberately shrinks both leaders to interchangeable labor.

"Ye are God's husbandry, ye are God's building" (v.9) relocates the Corinthians' identity from being someone's followers to belonging to God directly. Every leader they'd been ranking is, in this picture, just one worker among several on a project neither of them owns.

chapters.title: Building on the Foundation
chapters.teaser: Paul warns that what gets built on Christ will be tested by fire, regardless of how impressive it looked.
body: "If any man build upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, stubble; every man's work shall be made manifest: for the day shall declare it, because it shall be revealed by fire" (v.12–13). The materials range from lasting to flammable, and only exposure to fire reveals which is which.

"If any man's work shall be burned, he shall suffer loss: but he himself shall be saved; yet so as by fire" (v.15). Paul separates the builder's ultimate security from the quality of what they built — a distinction that softens the warning without removing its force, since real loss is still possible even for someone who remains saved.

chapters.title: You Are God's Temple
chapters.teaser: Paul tells the fractured congregation, collectively, that they are the place where God actually dwells.
body: "Know ye not that ye are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwelleth in you?" (v.16). The "ye" is plural throughout — this isn't a claim about individual bodies (that comes later, in chapter 6) but about the church as a corporate dwelling place.

"If any man defile the temple of God, him shall God destroy; for the temple of God is holy" (v.17) raises the stakes on the very divisions the letter opened with — factionalism isn't just bad manners, it's treated as damage to something sacred that the whole community shares.

chapters.title: All Things Are Yours
chapters.teaser: Paul reverses the boasting he's been correcting, showing the Corinthians they already own more than they realize.
body: "Let no man glory in men. For all things are yours; whether Paul, or Apollos, or Cephas...all are yours" (v.21–22). The leaders they'd been fighting over turn out to belong to them, not the other way around — possessing rather than being possessed by a favorite teacher.

"Ye are Christ's; and Christ is God's" (v.23) closes the chapter's argument with a chain of belonging that makes rival factions look small by comparison. Why compete over which teacher to claim, Paul implies, when the believer already belongs to — and inherits through — Christ himself?

chapters.title: Judged by One Judge
chapters.teaser: Paul dismisses both self-judgment and the Corinthians' judgment as beside the point.
body: "With me it is a very small thing that I should be judged of you, or of man's judgment: yea, I judge not mine own self...he that judgeth me is the Lord" (v.3–4). This isn't arrogance — Paul admits he isn't even confident in his own self-assessment, since "I know nothing by myself; yet am I not hereby justified."

"Judge nothing before the time, until the Lord come" (v.5) redirects the Corinthians' habit of ranking teachers — the very factionalism from chapter 1 — toward a future accounting they aren't equipped to render prematurely. Final verdicts, Paul insists, belong to someone else.

chapters.title: What You Didn't Earn
chapters.teaser: A single question punctures the Corinthians' pride in their own spiritual sophistication.
body: "Who maketh thee to differ from another? and what hast thou that thou didst not receive? now if thou didst receive it, why dost thou glory, as if thou hadst not received it?" (v.7). It's a compact, almost unanswerable challenge to anyone treating a gift as a personal achievement.

The question lands hardest against the backdrop of verses 8, where Paul notes with irony that the Corinthians already act as though they've "reigned as kings" — spiritually self-satisfied while their apostles, per the next verses, are living in genuine hardship.

chapters.title: Fools for Christ's Sake
chapters.teaser: Paul contrasts the apostles' actual suffering with the Corinthians' comfortable self-image.
body: "We are fools for Christ's sake, but ye are wise in Christ; we are weak, but ye are strong...even unto this present hour we both hunger, and thirst, and are naked, and are buffeted, and have no certain dwellingplace" (v.10–11). The contrast is drawn with heavy irony — the church living comfortably while its founders are treated as "the filth of the world" (v.13).

This list isn't self-pity; it's a deliberate mirror held up to a church too pleased with itself. The gap between apostolic hardship and Corinthian self-satisfaction becomes Paul's evidence that something in their self-assessment has drifted from reality.

chapters.title: A Father, Not Just Instructors
chapters.teaser: Paul distinguishes his relationship to the Corinthians from the many teachers who came after him.
body: "Though ye have ten thousand instructors in Christ, yet have ye not many fathers: for in Christ Jesus I have begotten you through the gospel" (v.15). Instructors can be plentiful and interchangeable; a father who begot you occupies a different, irreplaceable role.

"I write not these things to shame you, but as my beloved sons I warn you" (v.14) frames the chapter's sharp irony as discipline rooted in relationship, not detached criticism. The appeal that follows — "be ye followers of me" (v.16) — only makes sense from someone claiming that specific, founding bond.

chapters.title: A Rod or Love
chapters.teaser: Paul lets the Corinthians choose which tone his next visit will take.
body: "I will come to you shortly, if the Lord will, and will know, not the speech of them which are puffed up, but the power" (v.19). Paul signals he's not interested in whatever rhetorical performance the arrogant faction can offer — he wants to see what they can actually do.

"What will ye? shall I come unto you with a rod, or in love, and in the spirit of meekness?" (v.21) closes the chapter with the choice thrown back to the readers. It's a pointed way to end four chapters of correction — the next move, Paul says, depends on how they respond to this one.

chapters.title: A Sin Even Pagans Blush At
chapters.teaser: The church is scandalized less by the sin itself than by its own pride about tolerating it.
body: "It is reported commonly that there is fornication among you...that one should have his father's wife. And ye are puffed up, and have not rather mourned" (v.1–2). The situation Paul describes — likely a stepmother relationship — was considered shocking even by the loose sexual standards of the wider Greco-Roman world.

The real target of Paul's rebuke isn't only the man involved but the congregation's response: pride instead of grief. A church that had been fighting over which teacher to follow apparently found room to boast about its open-mindedness even here — tolerance mistaken for maturity.

chapters.title: A Little Leaven
chapters.teaser: Paul uses a bread-making image to argue that unaddressed sin doesn't stay contained.
body: "Know ye not that a little leaven leaveneth the whole lump? Purge out therefore the old leaven, that ye may be a new lump, as ye are unleavened" (v.6–7). Leaven works invisibly and thoroughly — a small amount transforms the whole batch, which is exactly Paul's point about tolerated sin in a community.

"Christ our passover is sacrificed for us" (v.7) ties the image to Passover's unleavened bread, when Israel purged leaven from their homes before the feast. Paul reframes church discipline as a kind of ongoing Passover housekeeping — not punitive cruelty, but keeping the community's life consistent with what it's celebrating.

chapters.title: Delivered to Satan, for Rescue
chapters.teaser: Paul's harshest-sounding instruction turns out to have a restorative goal.
body: "To deliver such an one unto Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus" (v.5). The language is startling, but the stated purpose is recovery, not abandonment — removal from the community's protection so consequences can do their corrective work.

This sits alongside chapter 3's warning about being "saved; yet so as by fire" — Paul repeatedly distinguishes between ultimate salvation and severe present consequences. Discipline, in his framework, aims at restoration even when its immediate form looks like exclusion.

chapters.title: Judging Insiders, Not Outsiders
chapters.teaser: Paul draws a clear boundary around who the church is actually responsible to evaluate.
body: "What have I to do to judge them also that are without? do not ye judge them that are within? But them that are without God judgeth" (v.12–13). This limits the scope of church discipline specifically to the community's own members, not a general campaign against the world's morality.

It's a clarifying boundary that keeps the chapter's severity from becoming something it isn't — not a call to police outsiders' behavior, but an internal standard for a community that claims a particular identity and is expected to live consistently with it.

chapters.title: Clearing Up a Misunderstanding
chapters.teaser: Paul corrects how an earlier letter's instruction had apparently been misread.
body: "I wrote unto you in an epistle not to company with fornicators: yet not altogether with the fornicators of this world...for then must ye needs go out of the world" (v.9–10). Some in Corinth had apparently taken Paul's earlier warning as a call to withdraw from society entirely.

"If any man that is called a brother be a fornicator...with such an one no not to eat" (v.11) narrows the instruction back to its intended target — professed believers living inconsistently with that profession, not a blanket avoidance of unbelievers. The correction shows Paul actively managing how his own letters were being applied.

chapters.title: Suing Each Other Before Pagans
chapters.teaser: Paul is stunned that believers are settling disputes in courts run by people outside the faith.
body: "Dare any of you, having a matter against another, go to law before the unjust, and not before the saints?" (v.1). The practice wasn't just impractical to Paul — it was a public contradiction, airing the church's internal conflicts before judges who had no stake in the community's values.

"There is utterly a fault among you, because ye go to law one with another. Why do ye not rather take wrong?" (v.7) pushes further than most readers expect — Paul would rather see believers absorb an injustice than escalate the dispute in a way that damages the church's witness.

chapters.title: You Will Judge Angels
chapters.teaser: Paul uses an astonishing future claim to shame the pettiness of present-day lawsuits.
body: "Know ye not that the saints shall judge the world?...Know ye not that we shall judge angels? how much more things that pertain to this life?" (v.2–3). The logic is proportional: if believers are destined for that scale of authority, surely ordinary disputes are within their competence to settle internally.

"Is it so, that there is not a wise man among you? no, not one that shall be able to judge between his brethren?" (v.5) turns the shame up further — a church so gifted, per chapter 1, that it lacks nothing (1:7), apparently couldn't produce a single person capable of mediating a dispute without resorting to outside courts.

chapters.title: Such Were Some of You
chapters.teaser: A blunt vice list is followed immediately by a declaration of changed identity.
body: "Neither fornicators, nor idolaters, nor adulterers...nor thieves, nor covetous, nor drunkards...shall inherit the kingdom of God. And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified" (v.9–11). The list is unflinching, but its purpose isn't condemnation — it's contrast.

The triple "but ye are" marks a real before-and-after. Paul isn't pretending the Corinthians' past didn't happen; he's insisting it no longer defines them — which raises the question the rest of the chapter presses: if that identity has changed, why does behavior in some areas still look unchanged?

chapters.title: Lawful but Not Helpful
chapters.teaser: Paul quotes a Corinthian slogan and immediately qualifies it.
body: "All things are lawful unto me, but all things are not expedient: all things are lawful for me, but I will not be brought under the power of any" (v.12). This looks like Paul citing a phrase the Corinthians were using to justify indulgence, then adding the limits it had been missing.

The qualification matters: permissibility isn't the only relevant question. Something can be technically allowed and still be unwise, or still risk enslaving the very freedom it claims to exercise — a distinction Paul returns to explicitly in chapters 8 and 10 regarding food offered to idols.

chapters.title: Bought With a Price
chapters.teaser: Paul grounds sexual ethics not in rule-keeping but in ownership.
body: "Know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you, which ye have of God, and ye are not your own? For ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body" (v.19–20). The argument isn't a list of prohibitions — it's a claim about whose property the body actually is.

This echoes chapter 3's temple language, now applied to the individual rather than the whole church — both readings held together rather than competing. Behavior, in this framing, isn't obedience to an external code so much as consistency with who actually owns the one behaving.

chapters.title: Good, but Not Required
chapters.teaser: Paul answers a specific question from a Corinthian letter, balancing celibacy against marriage.
body: "Now concerning the things whereof ye wrote unto me: It is good for a man not to touch a woman. Nevertheless, to avoid fornication, let every man have his own wife" (v.1–2). "Now concerning" signals Paul is responding point by point to questions the church had actually sent him — this chapter is a reply, not an unprompted sermon.

Some in Corinth had apparently swung toward an extreme asceticism, treating celibacy as the only truly spiritual option. Paul affirms celibacy's value without making it mandatory — a careful middle path between two overcorrections he seems to be navigating on both sides at once.

chapters.title: Mutual Authority
chapters.teaser: Paul describes marriage using a striking equality unusual for its time.
body: "The wife hath not power of her own body, but the husband: and likewise also the husband hath not power of his own body, but the wife" (v.4). Both halves of the sentence are given equal weight — a mutuality rare in ancient household codes, which typically framed authority as one-directional.

"Defraud ye not one the other, except it be with consent for a time" (v.5) extends the same balance to sexual intimacy within marriage — a shared decision, not one partner's unilateral claim. The chapter's marriage ethic consistently resists granting either spouse a one-sided advantage over the other.

chapters.title: If the Unbeliever Leaves
chapters.teaser: Paul gives practical guidance for marriages where only one spouse has become a believer.
body: "If any brother hath a wife that believeth not, and she be pleased to dwell with him, let him not put her away...But if the unbelieving depart, let him depart. A brother or a sister is not under bondage in such cases: but God hath called us to peace" (v.12–15).

"What knowest thou, O wife, whether thou shalt save thy husband?" (v.16) holds out hope for the marriage's spiritual impact without making that hope a trap — if the unbelieving spouse chooses to leave, the believer isn't obligated to fight to keep a marriage the other party has already abandoned.

chapters.title: Stay As You Were Called
chapters.teaser: Paul applies a general principle of contentment across circumcision, slavery, and marital status alike.
body: "As God hath distributed to every man, as the Lord hath called every one, so let him walk. And so ordain I in all churches" (v.17). This isn't indifference to circumstance — it's a claim that spiritual identity doesn't require a change in social position to be complete.

"Art thou called being a servant? care not for it: but if thou mayest be made free, use it rather" (v.21) shows the principle isn't rigid — freedom, where available, is still worth taking. The point is that a person's standing before God was never contingent on first fixing their social circumstances.

chapters.title: The Time Is Short
chapters.teaser: Paul reframes ordinary relationships and possessions in light of an approaching, urgent horizon.
body: "The time is short: it remaineth, that both they that have wives be as though they had none...and they that buy, as though they possessed not: for the fashion of this world passeth away" (v.29–31). This isn't detachment from life so much as holding it loosely, aware that present arrangements aren't permanent.

This eschatological urgency — echoing Romans 13's "the night is far spent" — explains why Paul, throughout the chapter, keeps circling back to a mild preference for singleness during "the present distress" (v.26) without ever making marriage wrong. Both states are legitimate; neither should consume more attention than the moment actually allows.

chapters.title: Knowledge Puffs Up, Love Builds Up
chapters.teaser: Paul opens the meat-offered-to-idols debate by contrasting two very different postures.
body: "We know that we all have knowledge. Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth" (v.1). This sets the terms for three chapters (8–10) on a genuinely divisive Corinthian issue: whether it's acceptable to eat meat that had been sacrificed to pagan gods before being sold in the market.

"If any man think that he knoweth any thing, he knoweth nothing yet as he ought to know" (v.2) undercuts confidence in correct doctrine alone. Being theologically right about idols, Paul warns, can still produce the wrong outcome if it isn't paired with concern for how that rightness lands on someone else.

chapters.title: An Idol Is Nothing
chapters.teaser: Paul affirms sound theology about idols before complicating what that theology permits in practice.
body: "We know that an idol is nothing in the world, and that there is none other God but one...to us there is but one God, the Father...and one Lord Jesus Christ" (v.4, 6). The doctrine here is uncontroversial and correct — pagan gods have no real existence.

But correct theology, Paul immediately shows, doesn't automatically settle the practical question, because not everyone in the church holds that theology with equal confidence — which is exactly the complication the rest of the chapter addresses.

chapters.title: Not Everyone Has This Knowledge
chapters.teaser: Paul points out that some believers still experience eating idol-meat as genuine spiritual compromise.
body: "There is not in every man that knowledge: for some with conscience of the idol unto this hour eat it as a thing offered unto an idol; and their conscience being weak is defiled" (v.7). For someone recently converted from idol worship, the food might not feel neutral at all — it might feel like participation in the old religion.

This is Paul taking conscience seriously as a real factor, not a problem to be argued out of existence. Correct information doesn't instantly rewire someone's felt sense of what an act means — and that gap matters for how the theologically confident should behave around the theologically unsettled.

chapters.title: A Brother Christ Died For
chapters.teaser: Paul measures the cost of "knowledgeable" freedom against the value Christ placed on the person it might harm.
body: "Through thy knowledge shall the weak brother perish, for whom Christ died?...When ye sin so against the brethren, and wound their weak conscience, ye sin against Christ" (v.11–12). The stakes are deliberately raised — not just hurt feelings, but potential spiritual harm to someone Christ died for.

The comparison is stark on purpose: whatever social or personal benefit comes from exercising a technically correct freedom, Paul weighs it against the value of a single person's spiritual wellbeing, and finds the freedom the lighter side of that scale.

chapters.title: A Vow Not to Eat Meat
chapters.teaser: Paul commits to a personal restriction, not because he must, but because someone else might be hurt.
body: "Wherefore, if meat make my brother to offend, I will eat no flesh while the world standeth, lest I make my brother to offend" (v.13). This is a striking personal pledge — Paul isn't just arguing theory, he's modeling the very self-limitation he's asking the Corinthians to consider.

The move sets up chapter 9's extended defense of Paul's voluntarily surrendered rights as an apostle — chapter 8's principle (restrict your freedom for someone else's sake) becomes chapter 9's autobiography, Paul using his own choices as living proof the principle is workable.

chapters.title: The Right He Refused to Use
chapters.teaser: Paul lists every apostolic privilege he's entitled to, then explains why he doesn't claim them.
body: "Have we not power to eat and to drink? Have we not power to lead about a sister, a wife...have not we power to forbear working?" (v.4–6). Paul methodically establishes his legitimate claim to financial support before revealing he's deliberately declined it: "we have not used this power" (v.12).

This chapter follows directly from chapter 8's principle of surrendering freedom for others' sake — Paul isn't just telling the Corinthians to limit themselves for weaker believers, he's showing them he's already been doing exactly that with his own well-established rights as an apostle.

chapters.title: Muzzling the Ox
chapters.teaser: Paul reaches back to an obscure agricultural law to justify paying those who preach.
body: "It is written in the law of Moses, Thou shalt not muzzle the mouth of the ox that treadeth out the corn. Doth God take care for oxen? Or saith he it altogether for our sakes?" (v.9–10). The original command protected a working animal's right to eat from the grain it was processing.

"They which preach the gospel should live of the gospel" (v.14) draws the human application: those who labor spiritually for a community have a legitimate claim on that community's material support. Paul establishes the principle firmly — precisely so his own refusal to use it reads as choice, not necessity.

chapters.title: All Things to All Men
chapters.teaser: Paul describes deliberately adapting his behavior to reach people across different backgrounds.
body: "Unto the Jews I became as a Jew...to them that are without law, as without law...To the weak became I as weak, that I might gain the weak: I am made all things to all men, that I might by all means save some" (v.20–22).

This isn't inconsistency — Paul is careful to note he's not "without law to God, but under the law to Christ" (v.21). The flexibility is strategic, not principle-free: adjusting cultural presentation while keeping the actual message and his own accountability to Christ fixed.

chapters.title: Running to Win
chapters.teaser: Paul compares the Christian life to an athlete's training, aimed at a prize that doesn't decay.
body: "They do it to obtain a corruptible crown; but we an incorruptible. I therefore so run, not as uncertainly; so fight I, not as one that beateth the air" (v.25–26). Ancient athletic crowns, woven from perishable leaves, provide the contrast — Corinth, near the site of the Isthmian games, would have known the image well.

"Every man that striveth for the mastery is temperate in all things" (v.25) points to training discipline as the model, not a one-time decision. Paul treats spiritual effort the way a serious athlete treats physical training: sustained, deliberate, and aimed at an actual outcome, not aimless motion.

chapters.title: Disciplining the Body
chapters.teaser: Paul admits even his own apostleship doesn't exempt him from the risk of disqualification.
body: "I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection: lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway" (v.27). The word translated "castaway" suggests being disqualified from the race just described — failing the very standard he preached to others.

This closes the chapter on a note of humility that undercuts any reading of Paul as immune to failure by virtue of his calling. The whole chapter's argument about surrendering rights ends with an admission that even the apostle himself has to stay disciplined, not just generous.

chapters.title: Baptized Into Moses
chapters.teaser: Paul reads Israel's wilderness story as a kind of preview of Christian sacraments and their limits.
body: "All our fathers were under the cloud, and all passed through the sea; and were all baptized unto Moses in the cloud and in the sea...they drank of that spiritual Rock that followed them: and that Rock was Christ" (v.1–4). Paul finds Christ already present in Israel's ancient story, not just anticipated by it.

"With many of them God was not well pleased: for they were overthrown in the wilderness" (v.5) is the pivot — participation in these dramatic, sacrament-like events didn't guarantee anyone's outcome. It's a direct challenge to any Corinthian assumption that baptism or communion functioned as automatic protection regardless of ongoing conduct.

chapters.title: Written for Our Admonition
chapters.teaser: Paul lists Israel's specific failures as deliberate warnings for his own readers.
body: "These things were our examples, to the intent we should not lust after evil things, as they also lusted...Neither let us commit fornication, as some of them committed, and fell in one day three and twenty thousand" (v.6, 8). The failures — idolatry, sexual immorality, testing Christ, murmuring — read almost as a checklist of Corinth's own current temptations.

"They are written for our admonition, upon whom the ends of the world are come" (v.11) treats ancient narrative as live instruction, not distant history. Paul isn't moralizing in the abstract — he's matching Israel's wilderness failures point for point against issues already surfacing in the Corinthian church.

chapters.title: A Way of Escape
chapters.teaser: Paul's famous promise about temptation arrives in the middle of a stern warning, not a comforting devotional.
body: "There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man: but God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape" (v.13). Read in context, this follows immediately after a list of Israel's collapses under temptation.

"Let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall" (v.12) is the verse right before it — confidence, not just temptation, is the danger being addressed. The promise of an "escape" isn't a guarantee of ease; it's a guarantee that failure, unlike Israel's, isn't inevitable.

chapters.title: You Cannot Drink Both Cups
chapters.teaser: Paul treats communion and pagan sacrifice as real participation, not symbolic gestures that don't matter.
body: "The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ?...Ye cannot drink the cup of the Lord, and the cup of devils: ye cannot be partakers of the Lord's table, and of the table of devils" (v.16, 21).

"The things which the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to devils, and not to God" (v.20) is a stronger claim than chapter 8's "an idol is nothing" might suggest on its own — the food itself may be neutral, but participating in the sacrificial meal is a real spiritual act with a real object, and it can't be shared between two altars at once.

chapters.title: To the Glory of God
chapters.teaser: Paul closes the meat debate with a single governing principle rather than a fixed rule.
body: "Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God. Give none offence, neither to the Jews, nor to the Gentiles, nor to the church of God" (v.31–32). After three chapters of case-by-case reasoning, Paul resists reducing the issue to a simple yes-or-no rule.

"Whatsoever is sold in the shambles, that eat, asking no question for conscience sake" (v.25) shows the practical outworking — freedom in ordinary cases, restraint the moment someone's conscience is directly implicated. The principle from verse 31 is meant to travel with the believer into situations no single rule could anticipate.

chapters.title: Coverings and Honor
chapters.teaser: Paul argues about head coverings using a dense, culturally specific logic of honor and shame.
body: "The head of every man is Christ; and the head of the woman is the man; and the head of Christ is God...every woman that prayeth or prophesieth with her head uncovered dishonoureth her head" (v.3–5). The argument is tightly wound around first-century Corinthian social codes about hair and covering as markers of respectability.

It's one of the letter's most culturally dense passages, resistant to easy universal application, but the underlying concern is recognizable: Paul cared that public worship not create unnecessary scandal or embarrassment within Corinth's own social expectations — order and honor mattered to him more than any particular fashion.

chapters.title: Not Without Each Other
chapters.teaser: Paul adds a qualifying note that balances the passage's earlier claims about headship.
body: "Nevertheless neither is the man without the woman, neither the woman without the man, in the Lord. For as the woman is of the man, even so is the man also by the woman; but all things of God" (v.11–12).

This "nevertheless" functions as a corrective within Paul's own argument — whatever hierarchy he's described, he immediately insists on mutual dependence rather than one-directional superiority. Origin (woman from man, in Genesis) is answered by ongoing reality (every man since born of a woman), and both are traced back to God as the common source.

chapters.title: Gathering for the Worse
chapters.teaser: Paul confronts a shared meal that had turned into a display of the rich excluding the poor.
body: "When ye come together therefore into one place, this is not to eat the Lord's supper. For in eating every one taketh before other his own supper: and one is hungry, and another is drunken" (v.20–21). The Lord's Supper had apparently been folded into a communal meal where wealthier members ate well while poorer members, arriving later from work, went hungry.

"Have ye not houses to eat and to drink in? or despise ye the church of God, and shame them that have not?" (v.22) makes clear this wasn't a minor etiquette breach — it was a betrayal of what the meal was supposed to represent, turning a symbol of unity into a display of social division.

chapters.title: This Do in Remembrance
chapters.teaser: Paul quotes what may be the earliest written account of the Last Supper's institution.
body: "I have received of the Lord that which also I delivered unto you, That the Lord Jesus the same night in which he was betrayed took bread...This do in remembrance of me" (v.23–24). Written likely in the mid-50s AD, this predates the Gospels' written accounts, making it possibly the oldest surviving record of the event.

"As often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord's death till he come" (v.26) frames the meal as ongoing proclamation, not just private remembrance — every observance is, in effect, a small sermon preached with bread and cup instead of words.

chapters.title: Examine Yourself
chapters.teaser: Paul asks believers to test their own hearts before joining a meal that's meant to unify, not divide.
body: "Let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread, and drink of that cup. For he that eateth and drinketh unworthily...eateth and drinketh damnation to himself, not discerning the Lord's body" (v.28–29).

"Discerning the Lord's body" likely carries a double meaning in this context — failing to recognize both the significance of Christ's sacrifice and the unity of the church itself, the very community being divided by the meal's abuse in verses 20–22. Self-examination, here, is inseparable from how one is treating the rest of the gathered church.

chapters.title: No One Calls Jesus Cursed
chapters.teaser: Paul offers a baseline test for distinguishing genuine Spirit-inspired speech from counterfeit.
body: "No man speaking by the Spirit of God calleth Jesus accursed: and...no man can say that Jesus is the Lord, but by the Holy Ghost" (v.3). In a church excited about spiritual experiences and dramatic speech, Paul provides a simple content check before anything else.

This grounds the entire discussion of spiritual gifts that follows in a basic confession — whatever impressive phenomena occur, the minimum test is whether they affirm Jesus as Lord. Gifts, however striking, aren't self-authenticating apart from that content.

chapters.title: Same Spirit, Different Gifts
chapters.teaser: Paul insists diversity among believers' gifts flows from one unified source, not competing rankings.
body: "There are diversities of gifts, but the same Spirit...the manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man to profit withal" (v.4, 7). The list that follows — wisdom, knowledge, faith, healing, miracles, prophecy, tongues, interpretation (v.8–10) — is deliberately varied, resisting any single gift as the standard everyone should aspire to.

"All these worketh that one and the selfsame Spirit, dividing to every man severally as he will" (v.11) places the distribution decision with the Spirit, not with individual ambition or church hierarchy — a direct counter to any ranking system the Corinthians might have been building around more visible or impressive gifts.

chapters.title: The Body Has Many Parts
chapters.teaser: Paul extends the body metaphor to answer members who feel their gift makes them inferior.
body: "If the foot shall say, Because I am not the hand, I am not of the body; is it therefore not of the body?...If the whole body were an eye, where were the hearing?" (v.15, 17). The image directly answers an insecurity Paul evidently expected — members comparing themselves unfavorably to more visible gifts.

"Now hath God set the members every one of them in the body, as it hath pleased him" (v.18) locates the design decision with God, not with the member's own preference or self-assessment. Diversity of function isn't an accident to be corrected — it's how the body was deliberately built to work.

chapters.title: I Have No Need of Thee
chapters.teaser: Paul confronts the opposite insecurity — members who look down on parts they consider less impressive.
body: "The eye cannot say unto the hand, I have no need of thee...those members of the body, which seem to be more feeble, are necessary...God hath tempered the body together, having given more abundant honour to that part which lacked" (v.21, 22, 24).

"That there should be no schism in the body; but that the members should have the same care one for another" (v.25) states the goal directly — not uniform gifting, but mutual care across genuine difference. The chapter answers both directions of comparison: don't feel inferior, and don't act superior.

chapters.title: A More Excellent Way
chapters.teaser: The chapter's final line pivots from gifts themselves to the spirit in which they should be exercised.
body: "Covet earnestly the best gifts: and yet shew I unto you a more excellent way" (v.31). After a whole chapter organizing gifts by diversity and mutual necessity, Paul signals that something even more foundational is coming.

That single transitional verse sets up chapter 13 — not a break from the topic of spiritual gifts but its deepest grounding. Whatever gift a believer has, Paul is about to argue, is worth nothing without the quality he's about to describe next.

chapters.title: Nothing Without Love
chapters.teaser: Paul renders even the most impressive spiritual gifts worthless without love attached.
body: "Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not charity, I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal...though I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and have not charity, I am nothing" (v.1–2).

This isn't a wedding poem in its original setting — it's a direct rebuke to a gifted, quarrelsome church that had just spent chapter 12 sorting out competing spiritual gifts. Tongues, prophecy, knowledge, faith, even radical self-sacrifice (v.3) are each measured against the same standard and each found empty without it.

chapters.title: What Love Actually Does
chapters.teaser: Paul defines love almost entirely through verbs of behavior rather than statements of feeling.
body: "Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up, doth not behave itself unseemly, seeketh not her own, is not easily provoked, thinketh no evil" (v.4–5). Every clause names an action or restraint, not an emotion.

Several of these phrases directly answer problems already surfacing in the letter — "vaunteth not itself" and "is not puffed up" recall the boasting of chapters 1, 4, and 5; "seeketh not her own" answers chapter 10's instruction to seek "another's wealth." The chapter isn't abstract poetry; it's a checklist against the Corinthians' own documented failures.

chapters.title: Love Never Fails
chapters.teaser: Paul contrasts love's permanence with the built-in expiration date of the flashier gifts.
body: "Charity never faileth: but whether there be prophecies, they shall fail; whether there be tongues, they shall cease; whether there be knowledge, it shall vanish away" (v.8). The gifts Corinth prized most — tongues, prophecy, special knowledge — are all described as temporary by nature, useful for now but not built to last.

"We know in part, and we prophesy in part" (v.9) explains why: these gifts are partial tools suited to an incomplete present, not permanent fixtures. Love's endurance, by contrast, isn't tied to the limitations the other gifts were designed to work within.

chapters.title: Through a Glass, Darkly
chapters.teaser: Paul compares present spiritual knowledge to a blurred reflection, not yet the real thing.
body: "Now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face: now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known" (v.12). Ancient mirrors, made of polished metal rather than glass, gave an imperfect, distorted reflection — a fitting image for partial understanding.

"When I became a man, I put away childish things" (v.11) frames the present spiritual gifts, however impressive, as a kind of childhood stage — genuinely useful, not to be despised, but destined to be outgrown once the fuller reality arrives.

chapters.title: The Greatest of These
chapters.teaser: Paul ranks love above even the virtues most central to Christian identity.
body: "Now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity" (v.13). Faith and hope, Paul implies elsewhere, are oriented toward what's not yet seen or possessed — they have a natural endpoint once their object is finally realized.

Love, by contrast, doesn't become obsolete once its goal arrives — it simply continues, unlike faith (which gives way to sight) and hope (which gives way to fulfillment). That's the quiet logic behind calling it "the greatest": not more important in a competition, but the one virtue that never runs out of a reason to exist.

chapters.title: Edifying Others, Not Just Yourself
chapters.teaser: Paul ranks prophecy above tongues specifically because it benefits the whole gathered church.
body: "He that speaketh in an unknown tongue speaketh not unto men, but unto God: for no man understandeth him...he that prophesieth speaketh unto men to edification, and exhortation, and comfort" (v.2–3). The comparison isn't about which gift is more spiritually impressive — it's about which one actually helps the people in the room.

"He that speaketh in an unknown tongue edifieth himself; but he that prophesieth edifieth the church" (v.4) makes the criterion explicit. This directly continues chapter 13's argument — a gift exercised without love for the gathered community, however genuine its origin, misses the point of communal worship.

chapters.title: An Uncertain Trumpet
chapters.teaser: Paul argues that unintelligible speech, however sincere, fails the basic purpose of communication.
body: "Things without life giving sound, whether pipe or harp, except they give a distinction in the sounds, how shall it be known what is piped or harped? For if the trumpet give an uncertain sound, who shall prepare himself to the battle?" (v.7–8). A trumpet's whole function collapses if its signal can't be understood.

"Ye shall speak into the air" (v.9) is the blunt verdict on speech no one present can understand. Paul isn't devaluing the experience of tongues itself — he's insisting that in a gathered, mixed assembly, intelligibility isn't optional if the goal is actually building others up.

chapters.title: Five Words With Understanding
chapters.teaser: Paul weighs his own extensive tongues experience against its practical usefulness to others.
body: "I thank my God, I speak with tongues more than ye all: yet in the church I had rather speak five words with my understanding, that by my voice I might teach others also, than ten thousand words in an unknown tongue" (v.18–19).

The comparison is deliberately lopsided — five intelligible words against ten thousand unintelligible ones — to make the point emphatically rather than subtly. Paul isn't dismissing the gift he claims to possess abundantly; he's ranking its public value against a much smaller but comprehensible alternative.

chapters.title: Order, Not Chaos
chapters.teaser: Paul lays out practical rules for a worship service with too many people wanting to speak at once.
body: "How is it then, brethren? when ye come together, every one of you hath a psalm, hath a doctrine, hath a tongue, hath a revelation, hath an interpretation. Let all things be done unto edifying" (v.26). The picture is of an enthusiastic, possibly chaotic gathering with everyone eager to contribute simultaneously.

"God is not the author of confusion, but of peace" (v.33) is the governing principle behind the specific instructions that follow — limiting the number of speakers, requiring interpretation, taking turns. The rules aren't suppression for its own sake; they're structure in service of a genuinely edifying, comprehensible gathering.

chapters.title: Decently and in Order
chapters.teaser: The chapter's closing line sums up its entire argument about worship in five words.
body: "Let all things be done decently and in order" (v.40). After specific instructions about tongues, prophecy, and turn-taking, Paul compresses the whole chapter's concern into a single closing principle.

This connects back to verse 23's concern for outsiders — "if therefore the whole church be come together...and all speak with tongues...will they not say that ye are mad?" Order, in Paul's argument, isn't about suppressing the Spirit's activity; it's about making sure worship remains legible and welcoming to whoever walks through the door, believer or not.

chapters.title: A Creed Received and Passed On
chapters.teaser: Paul quotes what scholars widely regard as an early Christian creed, predating this letter itself.
body: "I delivered unto you first of all that which I also received, how that Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures; and that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day...and that he was seen of Cephas, then of the twelve" (v.3–5).

"He was seen of above five hundred brethren at once; of whom the greater part remain unto this present" (v.6) is a striking detail — Paul essentially invites skeptical readers to go ask the eyewitnesses themselves, since most were apparently still alive when he wrote. The formulaic structure suggests this summary was already fixed tradition, recited and passed down before Paul ever wrote it here.

chapters.title: If Christ Be Not Raised
chapters.teaser: Paul traces out, step by step, everything that collapses if the resurrection didn't actually happen.
body: "If Christ be not risen, then is our preaching vain, and your faith is also vain...ye are yet in your sins...If in this life only we have hope in Christ, we are of all men most miserable" (v.14, 17, 19).

This is Paul refusing to treat the resurrection as a detachable add-on to Christian belief — he stakes the entire structure on its historical reality. The argument's severity is deliberate: some in Corinth apparently doubted a future resurrection while still claiming Christian faith, and Paul shows that position can't actually hold together.

chapters.title: Firstfruits
chapters.teaser: Paul frames Christ's resurrection as the first installment of a harvest still to come.
body: "Now is Christ risen from the dead, and become the firstfruits of them that slept. For since by man came death, by man came also the resurrection of the dead. For as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive" (v.20–22).

Firstfruits is an agricultural term — the first portion of a harvest, guaranteeing the rest is coming. The image reruns Romans 5's Adam/Christ comparison in a new key: not just righteousness versus condemnation, but death versus a resurrection already begun and proven, not merely promised.

chapters.title: Bare Grain
chapters.teaser: Paul uses a planted seed to explain how the resurrection body can be both continuous and utterly changed.
body: "That which thou sowest is not quickened, except it die...thou sowest not that body that shall be, but bare grain...But God giveth it a body as it hath pleased him" (v.36–38). A seed and the plant that grows from it are recognizably connected, yet look nothing alike.

"It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body" (v.44) applies the image directly — the resurrection body isn't a resuscitated corpse, nor a different person's replacement, but the same self transformed the way a buried seed becomes something the seed itself never visibly resembled.

chapters.title: Death Swallowed Up in Victory
chapters.teaser: The chapter's argument builds to a triumphant quotation aimed directly at death's power.
body: "So when this corruptible shall have put on incorruption...then shall be brought to pass the saying that is written, Death is swallowed up in victory. O death, where is thy sting?...The sting of death is sin; and the strength of sin is the law" (v.54–56).

"Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord" (v.58) closes the chapter with a practical payoff — the resurrection isn't just future comfort, it's the reason present effort and suffering, for Paul, aren't wasted.

chapters.title: The Collection, Week by Week
chapters.teaser: Paul gives practical instructions for regular giving that double as early evidence of Sunday gatherings.
body: "Upon the first day of the week let every one of you lay by him in store, as God hath prospered him, that there be no gatherings when I come" (v.2). This is a down-to-earth close to a letter that just spent a chapter on the resurrection — theology landing in weekly practicality.

The instruction also happens to be one of the earliest hints that Christians were gathering regularly on "the first day of the week" rather than the Jewish Sabbath, tied to the resurrection Paul just finished defending in chapter 15. The collection itself connects back to Romans 15's Jerusalem relief effort, part of the same larger project.

chapters.title: A Great Door, and Many Adversaries
chapters.teaser: Paul describes his ministry in Ephesus with opportunity and opposition held together in one sentence.
body: "I will tarry at Ephesus until Pentecost. For a great door and effectual is opened unto me, and there are many adversaries" (v.8–9). The two clauses sit side by side without resolving the tension — real fruitfulness and real resistance, simultaneously.

This is a candid glimpse of what ministry actually looked like for Paul — not a smooth string of successes, but genuine opportunity that came bundled with genuine cost. He doesn't treat the adversaries as a reason to leave the open door; both facts simply coexist in his plans.

chapters.title: Be Strong, in Love
chapters.teaser: Paul's closing charge pairs toughness with the very virtue chapter 13 spent a whole chapter defining.
body: "Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong. Let all your things be done with charity" (v.13–14). The exhortation to strength could sound harsh on its own; Paul immediately grounds it in love, refusing to let firmness become an excuse for coldness.

Placed at the very end of a letter that spent chapters correcting factionalism, sexual sin, lawsuits, and disorderly worship, this final pairing feels deliberate — strength without love produced exactly the kind of church Paul had been writing to fix.

chapters.title: Those Who Labored
chapters.teaser: Paul singles out a specific household for the practical support they gave him.
body: "I beseech you, brethren, (ye know the house of Stephanas, that it is the firstfruits of Achaia, and that they have addicted themselves to the ministry of the saints,)...I am glad of the coming of Stephanas and Fortunatus and Achaicus: for that which was lacking on your part they have supplied" (v.15, 17).

"They have refreshed my spirit and yours: therefore acknowledge ye them that are such" (v.18) is a small but pointed instruction — after chapters spent correcting the Corinthians' failures, Paul makes a point of publicly naming and honoring the people who quietly did their part well.

chapters.title: Anathema and Love, Side by Side
chapters.teaser: The letter's final lines hold a stark curse and a tender blessing in the same breath.
body: "If any man love not the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be Anathema Maranatha... My love be with you all in Christ Jesus. Amen" (v.22, 24). Maranatha, an Aramaic phrase meaning "our Lord, come," is one of the oldest prayers of the early church, preserved here in its original language.

The juxtaposition is jarring but fitting for a letter this direct — sixteen chapters spent naming hard problems by name, closing with both a warning for those outside genuine devotion to Christ and an unmistakably warm farewell for the church Paul had spent the whole letter trying to help.
